slides.title: Two small display features already have an order
keyPoints: Plain text begins as ready now.
A prefix adds WARN and a space.
A limit keeps at most five bytes of its input.
slides.narration: A status panel needs optional features around a basic message. One feature adds an alert prefix. Another keeps only the first five bytes of text. Some screens need both. Before naming a pattern, ask what the final screen should show, because prefixing and limiting can interact. If the limit runs first, the later prefix increases the visible length. If the prefix runs first, a later limit can cut the body away entirely. The chapter uses simple single-byte text, so these examples are easy to trace. A real Unicode layout requirement would need a separate definition of visible character boundaries.
actions: Ask learners to write the two possible transformation orders before seeing code.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch09.json → When two small features produce many variants

question.prompt: Why is the phrase prefix plus limit incomplete as a requirement?
question.answer: It does not state the order, and the two orders can produce different visible results.

slides.title: For one fixed policy, write the expression
keyPoints: Take the first five bytes of the body.
Then add the alert prefix.
A direct function needs no owned object chain.
slides.narration: This baseline has exactly one policy: trim the body first, then add the prefix. A single function makes that order visible. Substr starts at index zero and requests at most five bytes. The plus operation joins two strings, and the function returns the new string by value. The expected output includes quotes so the message boundary is visible. This approach is a good choice when every screen follows this same rule and no caller requires a Message object. We will introduce decorators only after independent runtime choices make a fixed expression too restrictive. Simpler code is still the correct outcome for a simpler requirement.
actions: Run the baseline and count the final bytes including the space.
slides.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch09.json → When two small features produce many variants

question.prompt: Does this baseline promise that the final message is at most five bytes?
question.answer: No. It limits the body first; the later prefix makes the final result longer.

slides.title: The same features can violate the final limit
keyPoints: Prefix after limit produces ten bytes.
Limit after prefix produces five bytes.
The surviving five bytes can be only the alert marker.
slides.narration: Now the requirement changes: the complete visible message must fit five bytes. Our baseline no longer meets it because it adds the prefix after the body was shortened. The demonstration prints both orders and their lengths. This is a safe, deterministic way to study the failure: nothing crashes, but one answer breaks the final-size rule. Moving the limit outside fixes that rule while raising a different product question: is an alert marker with no body useful? The design must state both constraints. A pattern can make order explicit, but it cannot decide which user-visible behavior is correct for the application.
actions: Predict both quoted outputs, including the trailing space.
Discuss whether preserving a warning marker matters more than preserving body text.
slides.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch09.json → Order is visible behavior

question.prompt: Which expression satisfies a final five-byte limit, and what does it discard?
question.answer: Limiting the already-prefixed string satisfies the bound; with WARN plus a space, it discards the entire body.

code.expectedStdout:
prefix last='WARN ready' size=10
limit last='WARN ' size=5

slides.title: Make each feature usable as a Message
keyPoints: Plain and wrappers all support text().
A wrapper holds one inner Message.
Another wrapper can therefore be the inner object.
slides.narration: When screens choose different combinations at runtime and clients expect Message objects, the fixed function is no longer the whole solution. A decorator implements the same public operation as the object it surrounds. Plain supplies the starting text. Prefix and Limit also implement Message, but each asks an inner Message for its result and then transforms that result. Because an inner Message can itself be another decorator, the arrangement can form a chain. This replaces a separate subclass for every combination with reusable features and explicit assembly. The important evidence is the preserved interface and delegated behavior, not merely the word wrapper in a class name.
actions: Name the basic component, common contract, and two wrappers.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch09.json → A wrapper with the same public operation

question.prompt: Why is inner_ typed as Message rather than Plain?
question.answer: It must accept another decorator as well as a plain message so that features can nest.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Support plain text, prefixing, and a length limit.
Permit either wrapper order through Message::text.
Reject a wrapper with no inner object and preserve empty-string behavior.
slides.narration:
Two ways to decorate a status message. Each wrapper owns exactly one Message and implements the same query. Ownership makes the assembled chain self-contained; explicit nesting makes order reviewable.

Support plain text, prefixing, and a length limit. Permit either wrapper order through Message::text. Reject a wrapper with no inner object and preserve empty-string behavior.

Every wrapper has one non-null inner owner. text returns a new value and does not mutate the chain. Limit applies to the complete result returned by its immediate inner object. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. A pair of string functions is better for one fixed transformation sequence. A vector of transformation functions fits a pipeline that does not otherwise need a Message object interface.

comparisons.label: Chosen design
comparisons.text: Each wrapper owns exactly one Message and implements the same query. Ownership makes the assembled chain self-contained; explicit nesting makes order reviewable.

comparisons.label: A reasonable alternative
comparisons.text: A pair of string functions is better for one fixed transformation sequence. A vector of transformation functions fits a pipeline that does not otherwise need a Message object interface.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Decorator implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: Every wrapper has one non-null inner owner. text returns a new value and does not mutate the chain. Limit applies to the complete result returned by its immediate inner object.

slides.narration:
A status panel starts with plain text such as ready now. Some screens add WARN before the text. Some limit the display to five characters. A screen may need both behaviors, and its policy must say which applies first. For this chapter, strings contain simple single-byte characters. The program is not a full Unicode layout engine.

With one fixed policy, a direct expression is the simplest implementation. Add the prefix and take a substring. That clearly states the order. The problem appears when screens choose different combinations at runtime. Classes named PrefixedMessage, LimitedMessage, PrefixedLimitedMessage, and LimitedPrefixedMessage repeat pieces of behavior. Adding a suffix or a timestamp creates more combinations. We need reusable features that can be assembled without defining a new class for every pairing.

std::string displayed = ("WARN " + text).substr(0, 5);

question.answer: Trimming the prefixed result can remove part of the original message or suffix. Trimming the original first leaves the later prefix outside the limit. Order is part of the requirement, not an implementation detail.

slides.title: A wrapper with the same public operation
keyPoints: A decorator is an object that adds behavior around another object while keeping the same interface.
The important fact is that every layer remains usable as a Message.
We do not add a generic Decorator base class merely to repeat the inner_ member.
slides.narration:
A decorator is an object that adds behavior around another object while keeping the same interface. Message provides text(). Plain returns its stored text. Prefix and Limit are also Messages, but each owns an inner Message and calls that object's text before adding its own behavior. Since the inner object may itself be another decorator, the same construction rule supports a chain of features.

The important fact is that every layer remains usable as a Message. This is why the common interface is needed now: callers must accept an assembled chain without knowing its exact shape. Public inheritance supplies that substitutability. Containing an inner Message supplies the behavior being extended. The inheritance link and the ownership link answer different questions and must remain distinct in the diagram.

We do not add a generic Decorator base class merely to repeat the inner_ member. Two small wrappers do not yet need that additional inheritance layer. If many wrappers later share forwarding behavior and validation, a base wrapper can remove useful duplication. First show the repeated need; then judge whether sharing that implementation makes the code easier to change.

slides.title: Order is visible behavior
keyPoints: The first chain is Prefix around Limit around Plain.
The second chain is Limit around Prefix around Plain.
Operations whose order changes the result are noncommutative: swapping them changes behavior.
slides.narration:
The first chain is Prefix around Limit around Plain. A call enters Prefix, which asks Limit for text. Limit asks Plain and receives ready now. Limit keeps the first five characters, ready, and returns them. Prefix then adds WARN and returns WARN ready. The five-character rule applied only to the inner body, so the final string is longer than five.

The second chain is Limit around Prefix around Plain. Plain again returns ready now. Prefix returns WARN ready now. The outer Limit keeps its first five characters: W, A, R, N, and a space. The printed single quotes make the trailing space visible. The final result is 'WARN '. This is not an implementation accident. The outermost operation runs last on the returned text in this design.

Operations whose order changes the result are noncommutative: swapping them changes behavior. Prefix and Limit are a concrete example. Never document a stack merely as 'prefix plus limit' if the order matters. Show the nesting or the actual transformation sequence. For logging, validation, caching, and compression wrappers in real systems, a wrong order can matter much more than a shortened message.

slides.title: Follow ownership separately from the call stack
keyPoints: Each wrapper stores unique_ptr<Message>.
make_unique constructs each object and returns its owner.
During text(), each layer also creates local strings.
Message explicitly allows default construction but deletes copy and move construction and assignment.
slides.narration:
Each wrapper stores unique_ptr<Message>. Its constructor receives an owner by value and moves that owner into inner_. The caller gives up ownership as part of construction. A null pointer is rejected immediately, so text can safely call inner_->text without a null check on every request. If construction throws, the already-initialized member owner cleans up its inner object automatically.

make_unique constructs each object and returns its owner. main nests those calls from the plain object outward. When first is destroyed, its Prefix is destroyed, which destroys its inner Limit, which destroys its Plain. Message has a virtual destructor so deleting through unique_ptr<Message> reaches the correct derived destructor. No caller needs to remember the chain's exact concrete types to clean it up.

During text(), each layer also creates local strings. body receives the inner result by value; result stores this layer's transformed text. These values own their character storage, so the method never returns a reference to a local string. Returning a string value permits safe transfer of the result to the caller. The chain's object lifetime is much longer than each local string's lifetime, and the two should not be confused.

Message explicitly allows default construction but deletes copy and move construction and assignment. The = delete notation asks the compiler to reject those operations. Derived wrappers therefore cannot be moved as whole objects, which would empty inner_ in the source and violate its non-null rule. Move the owning unique_ptr handle instead: ownership changes hands while the wrapper object and its inner chain stay in place. Compile-time static_assert checks use the type traits from <type_traits> to verify that Prefix and Limit cannot be copied or moved. The Suffix solution checks the same property. A type trait is a library query about a type; static_assert rejects a false condition during compilation.

slides.title: Syntax, cost, and boundary assumptions
keyPoints: The compiler verifies that every concrete Message implements text() const with the right return type.
At execution, virtual dispatch chooses each layer and each layer delegates once.
A chain with many layers may allocate and copy many intermediate strings.
Decorator is useful when features are independently selectable and have a consistent component contract.
slides.narration:
The compiler verifies that every concrete Message implements text() const with the right return type. override makes the check explicit. const permits reading through a const Message reference and promises not to alter the object through that method's ordinary members. It does not automatically make an arbitrary chain thread-safe if future decorators introduce mutable caches or shared services.

At execution, virtual dispatch chooses each layer and each layer delegates once. substr(0, limit_) begins at position zero and takes at most limit_ characters. If the requested length is larger than the body, it returns the whole body. A zero limit returns an empty string. std::size_t is an unsigned size type; a negative signed value converted to it would become a large positive size. The program constructs limits from nonnegative literals, and a user-input interface would need to reject negative values before conversion.

A chain with many layers may allocate and copy many intermediate strings. This example favors clarity over a claim of best performance. A fixed transformation pipeline made of ordinary functions can be simpler and cheaper when callers do not need objects sharing an interface. A streaming design may avoid large intermediates, but then each layer must define how it handles partial input and failures.

Decorator is useful when features are independently selectable and have a consistent component contract. It is less useful when the features depend on many details of one another or when an object needs a radically different interface. Keep the assembly code readable, test the important orders, and document whether repeated decoration is meaningful. Applying Prefix twice adds two prefixes; it is not automatically idempotent, meaning it does not necessarily leave the result unchanged after the first application.

question.prompt: What ownership action happens when the outermost wrapper is destroyed?
question.answer: Its unique_ptr destroys the inner object, which destroys its own inner object in turn. Virtual destructors allow deletion through Message to reach the actual types.

slides.title: Calls travel inward; text returns outward
keyPoints: Prefix asks Limit, which asks Plain.
Each layer transforms the returned value.
The outermost transformation runs last.
slides.narration: The outer object receives the first call, but that does not mean its transformation happens first. Prefix calls its inner object before joining its prefix. If that inner object is Limit, Limit first calls Plain, obtains ready now, and returns ready. Prefix then returns WARN ready. Reversing the wrapper nesting changes which intermediate string reaches Limit. The outer Limit receives WARN ready now and keeps only WARN plus a space. Trace the call direction and the return-value direction separately. This is a useful debugging habit in middleware too, because actions before delegation and actions after delegation can have very different orders.
actions: Trace calls inward using one color and returned strings outward using another.

question.prompt: Which operation runs last on the returned text in Prefix(Limit(Plain))?
question.answer: Prefix adds its text after Limit has already shortened the body.

theory.what: Nested components delegate once, then transform the returned value.
theory.why: Independent features can combine without one class per combination.
theory.invariant: Each wrapper applies its documented transformation at the stated point.
theory.risk: Reading construction order as transformation order predicts the wrong output.

slides.title: Same interface, different responsibility
keyPoints: Wrappers inherit Message to remain substitutable.
Each wrapper owns one inner Message.
The chain is a one-child structure, not a child collection.
slides.narration: A Prefix has two relationships with Message. It is usable as a Message because it publicly implements the interface. It also owns another Message through inner_. These relationships answer different questions. Inheritance says what calls the outer object can receive. Ownership says who keeps the inner object alive and destroys it. The diagram's inheritance triangle must not be read as an ownership arrow. Compared with Composite, this chapter's wrapper delegates through one inner component instead of combining a collection of children. Similar recursive shapes can therefore serve different intentions. Decorator adds a feature while keeping the component contract available for the next wrapper.
actions: Identify one inheritance link and one owning link in the actual diagram.

question.prompt: How does the child relationship differ from the Work Group in Composite?
question.answer: Each decorator owns one inner Message; a Composite Group owns a collection of Work children and combines their results.

theory.what: A wrapper both implements and owns a connection to the component contract.
theory.where: Prefix and Limit derive from Message and hold unique_ptr<Message>.
theory.why: A wrapped combination must still be acceptable wherever Message is expected.
theory.invariant: Every wrapper has one valid inner component.
theory.risk: Fixing inner_ to Plain would prevent wrapper nesting.

slides.title: Reject missing components during assembly
keyPoints: Move a unique owner into inner_.
Throw if inner_ is null.
Completed members clean up automatically on failure.
slides.narration: A wrapper cannot add behavior around nothing, so its constructor rejects a missing inner owner. The constructor receives a unique_ptr by value, then moves it into the member. That transfer records who is responsible for the inner object's lifetime. If validation throws, C++ destroys completed member objects, and the owning pointer cleans up its child automatically. In ordinary construction, nested make_unique calls build the chain from the inside outward. Destruction follows the ownership links inward when the outer owner disappears. Message needs a virtual destructor so deleting through the common base pointer reaches each actual derived object correctly.
actions: Trace a null constructor attempt and identify what exists when it throws.

question.prompt: Why is checking for null once in the constructor valuable?
question.answer: It establishes the invariant that every successfully constructed wrapper can delegate to an inner object.

theory.what: Assembly transfers exclusive ownership and rejects an unusable chain.
theory.why: Repeated text calls should not encounter a missing required component.
theory.invariant: Every living usable wrapper holds a non-null owner.
theory.risk: Accepting null turns a later text call into invalid pointer access.

slides.title: Move handles without moving service objects
keyPoints: Message deletes object copy and move operations.
Owning unique_ptr handles remain movable.
static_assert verifies wrapper type properties.
slides.narration: The chapter makes a careful distinction between moving an owner and moving the object it owns. A default move of a wrapper's unique_ptr member could leave the source wrapper with a null inner pointer, breaking its class invariant. Message therefore deletes copy and move operations, and the wrappers inherit that restriction. Equals delete means an attempted use is rejected during compilation. The outer unique_ptr handle can still move to a new owner while the wrapper stays at the same object location with its inner chain intact. Static assertions verify these type properties at build time. This is a policy choice that keeps the set of valid wrapper states small.
actions: Compare moving the outer unique_ptr variable with moving the Prefix object itself.

question.prompt: Why can moving a unique_ptr<Prefix> be safe while moving a Prefix object is disabled?
question.answer: Moving the handle transfers ownership of the same intact object; moving the object could empty its required inner owner.

theory.what: The program transfers ownership handles while preserving valid wrapper objects.
theory.where: Deleted Message special members and the wrapper static_assert checks.
theory.why: Moved-from service objects would otherwise need a separate supported state.
theory.invariant: A wrapper object retains its non-null component for its usable lifetime.
theory.risk: Adding an object move operation without a moved-from contract can break text().

slides.title: Returned strings are values with their own lives
keyPoints: text() returns a string value, not a local reference.
substr uses a start position and count.
Suffix should be tested inside and outside Limit.
slides.narration: Each call creates temporary local strings while the longer-lived message chain remains in place. Returning a string value safely gives the result to the caller. Returning a reference to a local result would instead leave the caller referring to destroyed storage. Substr takes a starting position followed by a maximum count; reversing their purpose can produce an empty result or an out-of-range error. The lab's Suffix follows the same ownership contract while appending text after delegation. Test it on both sides of Limit, because a suffix may be removed by an outer limit or extend a result after an inner limit. Reusing the interface does not remove interaction tests.

keyPoints: Read the ownership relationships in the named example.
Every wrapper has one non-null inner owner.
text returns a new value and does not mutate the chain.
slides.narration:
The ownership chain shown is first, where Prefix owns Limit and Limit owns Plain. The second chain reverses the wrapper order. Triangles describe type substitutability; ownership arrows describe who destroys which object. Calls travel inward and results return outward.

question.prompt: Explain Decorator without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Each wrapper owns exactly one Message and implements the same query. Ownership makes the assembled chain self-contained; explicit nesting makes order reviewable. A pair of string functions is better for one fixed transformation sequence. A vector of transformation functions fits a pipeline that does not otherwise need a Message object interface.

slides.title: Order and repetition are part of the API
keyPoints: Prefix and Limit do not commute.
Two prefixes usually produce two markers.
A limit is measured in the stated unit.
slides.narration: Two operations commute when swapping them preserves the result. Our prefix and limit do not, as the visible outputs demonstrate. Repetition is another question. An operation is idempotent when applying it again has the same effect as applying it once. Applying the same plain length limit again is idempotent for this text rule, but adding the prefix again adds another marker. These properties belong in the usage contract because a configuration system might accidentally repeat or reorder features. Also keep the unit precise: the current std::string operation counts bytes. A requirement phrased in displayed characters needs more design before it can safely reuse the same implementation.
actions: Ask learners which of Prefix and Limit is idempotent under the chapter rules.

slides.title: Similar wrappers can have different purposes
keyPoints: Decorator composes optional behavior.
Adapter translates an incompatible contract.
Proxy controls access to a represented service.
slides.narration: Wrapping another object appears in several patterns. To identify Decorator, ask whether the outer object preserves the component contract so that optional features can be nested. Adapter exists because two contracts disagree; translation is its central responsibility. Proxy represents another service and controls access, perhaps through permission checks or delayed construction. A diagram alone may not show the intent, and real designs can combine responsibilities. For this message program, the useful change is to add Suffix without rewriting Prefix, Limit, or the callers. If every screen forever uses one fixed sequence, direct string functions remain a simpler competing design.
actions: Give a permission-checking service wrapper and ask what fact would distinguish Proxy from Decorator.

slides.title: Explain a new layer before writing it
keyPoints: State what changes before or after delegation.
Preserve one non-null inner owner.
Test boundary inputs and important wrapper orders.
slides.narration: For your final explanation, propose a wrapper that replaces an empty message with the word unknown. First define whether empty means the inner result is empty or the original plain body was empty; the wrapper can directly observe only its immediate inner result. Then decide how it behaves inside and outside Limit with a zero limit. Those arrangements can disagree just as prefix and limit do. A good implementation plan states the common text contract, ownership rule, and observable transformation before showing code. This habit keeps new wrappers understandable and makes tests describe real behavior instead of merely checking that a class was constructed.

question.prompt: Why must a new wrapper describe which intermediate text it examines?
question.answer: It sees its immediate inner result, which may already have been changed by other wrappers; order changes that input.
